issues.legal_issue: An oral family arrangement followed by a writing that merely records the completed arrangement for the information of a court or revenue authority does not require compulsory registration.
material_facts: The parties reached an oral family arrangement before filing a petition for mutation of the land records.
The petition stated that a compromise had already been made and asked the revenue authority to mutate the parties’ names according to their allotted properties.
The parties had sought an adjournment while the compromise was being made, and the petition did not itself create or declare rights in the properties.
issues.conclusion: The oral arrangement was not required to be registered, and the later petition was only a memorandum of it; the arrangement could therefore be relied upon.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, registration is required when a writing itself creates or declares rights in immovable property, not when the parties first settle orally and later prepare a memorandum solely to record the settlement or inform a court. Tek Bahadur Bhujil v. Devi Singh; Ram Gopal v. Tulshi Ram; and the court’s discussion of Sitala Baksh Singh, Mst. Kalawati, Bakhtawar, and Awadh Narain Singh support this distinction.

predicates.family_arrangement_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a settlement among family members resolving property disputes is effective.
predicates.arrangement_completed_orally: The parties completed their settlement orally before preparing the later writing.
predicates.later_writing_only_records_settlement: The later writing merely reports the completed settlement to a court or authority and does not itself create or declare property rights.

issues.definition: When a family-property dispute involves a settlement completed orally and a later writing that only records it, the writing is not compulsorily registrable.

issues.legal_issue: A bona fide and voluntary family arrangement that fairly resolves family disputes may bind its parties even when a recipient lacks a legal title, if the arrangement recognizes a possible claim or the other parties relinquish their claims in that recipient’s favour.
material_facts: The settlement divided the properties among close members of the deceased owner’s family and gave the recipient a share despite his not then having a certain legal right to inherit while one of the daughters was alive.
The recipient was a grandson and prospective heir, and the daughters relinquished their claims to the properties allotted to him.
The arrangement gave the daughters permanent rights in their allotted properties and was considered fair and equitable in the circumstances.
The parties acted upon the settlement, and the respondents neither pleaded nor proved fraud, coercion, or undue influence.
issues.conclusion: The arrangement was bona fide, fair, and binding; the recipient’s possible claim and the relinquishment in his favour were sufficient to support it, and the challenge to its validity failed.
issues.legal_principle: Family arrangements are governed by a special equitable approach and are favoured when honestly made to settle present or possible family disputes. The parties need not all hold an established legal title: a possible claim may suffice, and a title may be assumed where another party relinquishes claims and acknowledges the recipient’s entitlement. The settlement must be bona fide and voluntary, and allegations of fraud or undue influence must be clearly pleaded and proved. Lala Khunni Lal v. Kunwar Gobind Krishna Narain; Mt. Hiran Bibi v. Mt. Sohan Bibi; Sahu Madho Das v. Pandit Mukand Ram; Ram Charan Das v. Girjanandini Devi; Tek Bahadur Bhujil v. Devi Singh; Maturi Pullaiah v. Maturi Narasimham; Krishna Biharilal v. Gulabchand; S. Shanmugam Pillai v. K. Shanmugam Pillai; and Ramgouda Annagouda v. Bhausaheb.

rule.if: family_arrangement_dispute and bona_fide_equitable_settlement and voluntary_agreement and possible_family_claim_acknowledged and no_fraud_or_undue_influence_proved

predicates.family_arrangement_dispute: The proceeding concerns an agreement among family members intended to settle disputes about family property.
predicates.bona_fide_equitable_settlement: The parties made a genuine settlement that fairly allotted property and resolved their competing claims.
predicates.voluntary_agreement: The parties agreed to the settlement voluntarily rather than under coercion or undue influence.
predicates.possible_family_claim_acknowledged: A recipient had a possible family claim, or the other parties relinquished their claims and acknowledged the recipient’s entitlement.
predicates.no_fraud_or_undue_influence_proved: The party challenging the agreement did not establish fraud or undue influence through properly pleaded and proved allegations.

issues.definition: A family-property settlement is binding when it was genuinely and fairly made voluntarily, recognized a possible family claim, and was not shown to have resulted from fraud or undue influence.

issues.legal_issue: A party to a family arrangement who has accepted and enjoyed benefits under it may be estopped from denying or challenging the arrangement, even assuming the arrangement was compulsorily registrable.
material_facts: The respondents signed the petition seeking mutation according to the settlement and received the properties allotted to them.
The parties remained in possession of their respective allotted properties and paid land revenue for several years without challenging the settlement.

The respondents later sought to displace the settlement in the consolidation proceedings; they had not filed objections when the relevant correction-of-records process provided an opportunity to do so.
issues.conclusion: The respondents were estopped from denying the existence or validity of the arrangement after taking its benefits; the majority applied estoppel even on the assumption that registration was required.
issues.legal_principle: Equitable estoppel prevents a party who accepted a family arrangement and obtained benefits under it from later resiling from or challenging it. The majority held that this principle applied even assuming the arrangement was compulsorily registrable. Kanhai Lal v. Brij Lal; Dhiyan Singh v. Jugal Kishore; Ram Charan Das v. Girjanandini Devi; Krishna Biharilal v. Gulabchand; and S. Shanmugam Pillai v. K. Shanmugam Pillai. Justice Sarkaria agreed that the appeal should be allowed but reserved his opinion on this alternative estoppel proposition.

predicates.family_arrangement_dispute: The proceeding concerns a family arrangement that resolved a dispute about property.
predicates.party_accepted_arrangement_benefits: A party accepted the arrangement and enjoyed the property or other benefits allotted under it.
predicates.party_later_challenges_arrangement: That party later sought to deny the arrangement or invalidate its effect.

issues.definition: A party to a family arrangement who accepted its benefits and later challenges it is prevented from resiling from the arrangement.
